title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
prompt: Given an integer array `nums`, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence is derived from the array by deleting zero or more elements without changing the relative order of the remaining elements; the remaining elements do not need to be contiguous.

examples.explanation: The longest increasing subsequence is [2,3,7,101] (or [2,3,7,18]), with length 4.
All elements are equal, and the sequence must be strictly increasing, so the best is any single element.

hints: For each index i, consider: what is the longest increasing subsequence that ENDS exactly at i?
Define dp[i] = length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at index i. dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j] for all j < i where nums[j] < nums[i]), or just 1 if no such j exists.

This naive approach is O(n^2), which is plenty for the given constraints. For a further challenge, an O(n log n) approach maintains a list of 'smallest tail values' for increasing subsequences of each length, using binary search to place each new value.

solution.approach: Use dynamic programming where dp[i] represents the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that ends at index i. Initialize every dp[i] to 1 (a single element is always a valid subsequence of length 1). For each i, look back at every j < i: if nums[j] < nums[i], then nums[i] could extend the subsequence ending at j, so dp[i] = max(dp[i], dp[j] + 1). The answer is the maximum value in dp.
